div.p: The global burden of heart failure (HF) has been esImated as affecIng more than 64 million people and presents as a significant socioeconomic burden for health care systems. Its prevalence is increasing due to a growing demographic of the aged. PaIents typically have poor prognoses, hence idenIfying individuals at a higher risk of adverse outcomes and novel targets for intervenIons are much desired. The paper from Wei et al (2023) 1 , now adds to a growing evidence base that Increased circulaIng levels of phenylacetylglutamine (PAGln), a microbial metabolite, can be used as a predicIve risk measure for cardiovascular events in HF paIents.

The average human is home to over by 3.8•10 13 microbes, mainly prokaryotes, the majority of which live in the gut. Historically, the thesis that some bacteria were beneficial to human health and could promote health span, was first proposed by Metchnikoff as early as 1908 2 . In recent Imes, it has become increasingly clear that humans and their microbiota maintain a highly complex inter-relaIonship and form a composite organism, termed a 'holobiont'. A dysbioIc, or perturbed microbiota, disrupts this inter-relaIonship, typically resulIng in a plethora of adverse health effects, as both physiological ecosystems and homeostasis are altered. Notably, imbalance in the relaIve composiIon of both salutobionts (i.e. health beneficial) and pathobionts (i.e. non-beneficial to health ) within the microbiota can predispose to and progress morbidiIes, such as cardio-renal disease and immune dysfuncIon 3 .

Over the anthropocene, the emergence of an industrialized human microbiota that has outpaced its natural symbioIc evoluIon as part of the holobiont it forms with humans, presents as a dangerous unknown for health. This is already apparent in its link to accelerated ageing and the prevalence of renal impairment 4,5 . Dysregulated ageing is a common underpinning feature of the non-communicable diseases (NCCDs) within the diseaseome of ageing. A recent meta-analysis of metagenomics datasets has found that ageing is a major confounder in studies linking the microbiota to disease. AddiIonally, in NCCDs dysbiosis of the gut microbiota plays a key role in inflammageing, as proinflammatory microbial metabolites contribute to vascular damage, disrupt cytokine networks and impair DNA damage repair mechanisms. This is perInent, as 10% of the metabolites found in blood are derived from the microbiota. An improved understanding of host-microbiota interacIons has emerged with the implementaIon of mulI-omic technologies, including metagenomic sequencing, meta-transcriptomics, meta-proteomics and crucially metabolomics. A range of microbiota-derived metabolites, including trimethylamine ( and its derivaIve trimethylamine N-oxide) short-chain fady acids, indole derivaIves, bile acids, branchedchain amino acids and tryptophan have already been implicated in the pathogenesis of a range of metabolic disorders. The present study from Wei et al. 1 adds to this body of evidence and shows clinically that PAGln levels can track HF risk.

Previous studies have idenIfied an associaIon between PAGln levels and CVD in both US and European cohorts 7 mediated through interacIon with adrenergic receptors. More recently, systemic PAGln levels have been shown to dose-dependently track both with HF risks and a range of indices of HF severity, in separate clinical cohorts, independently of the tradiIonal cardiovascular risk factors, renal funcIon, ejecIon fracIon, and NT-proBNP level 7 . Elevated PAGln levels have also been associated with a higher risk of cardiovascular death in heart failure with reduced ejecIon fracIon (HFrEF); however, these studies were limited in size and follow-up period 8 . AddiIonally, the associaIon between PAGln and the classical biomarker NT-proBNP remained to be fully addressed.

Wei et al have now sought to expand on these previous studies, using a prospecIve large Chinese cohort study (n=3125) to address the associaIon between PAGln and the subtypes of HF and any the connecIon between plasma PAGln and β-blocker use in HF paIents. These authors demonstrate, that in this geographically and ethnically disInct cohort, the relaIonship between PAGLn levels and HF remains robust, even aler adjusIng for NT-proBNP levels and classical confounding factors, such as age and renal funcIon. They have confirmed the predicIve value of PAGln for HF, demonstraIng that higher plasma PAGln levels independently predict a higher risk of cardiovascular death, or heart transplantaIon, in both HFrEF and HFpEF paIents.

Clinically, using PAGln combined with NT-proBNP may even improve paIent risk straIficaIon among HF paIents presenIng with even low NT-proBNP levels. There is already an increasing body of evidence highlighIng low or normal BNP/NT-proBNP levels in those presenIng with HFpEF which exhibit an increased risk of death or hospital readmission 9 . In keeping with this thesis, in the current study, over 90% of those displaying HFpEF had low NT-proBNP levels, highlighIng the potenIal for combining PAGln with NT-proBNP.

MechanisIcally, the observaIon that PAGln promoted the expression of IL-1β and IL-6 in the presence of ISO is in keeping with the idea that PAGln increases the inflammatory response in HF, supporIng iniIal observaIons indicaIng that PAGln deteriorates myocardial inflammatory cell infiltraIon in pressure overload-induced HF in mice. Metagenomic analyses have already provided potenIal mechanisIc insight and idenIfied bacteria encoding the por a sequence, a key enzyme required for PAGln synthesis, in paIents with atrial fibrillaIon, suggesIng a novel target for intervenIon. A proven mechanisIc link between the NLRP3 inflammasome-related inflammatory pathways and the proinflammatory microbial metabolite trimethylamine-N-oxide has already been described for cardiovascular disease. Combining use of PAGln and TMAO as biomarkers for HF, may thus prove useful clinically, as studies looking at TMAO have shown that this metabolite contributes to myocardial fibrosis, reduced LV funcIon and adverse cardiac remodelling. Significantly, these effects could be reversed by drugs targeIng microbial pathways involved in TMA generaIon. A similar approach for PAGln might also prove fruioul.

Another perInent observaIon from this study was the lack of associaIon between PAGln and medicaIon use, including the use of β-blockers, diureIcs and ACEI/ARB. The reasons for this remain to be determined, but it is worth considering the limitaIons of this study. In this respect, the lack of measurement of any dynamic changes in PAGln and a lack of both dietary and microbiota data related to PAGln producIon are likely to prove crucial. This is perInent to observaIons of accelerated ageing and poorer cardiac and renal health in the general populaIon associated with lower socioeconomic posiIon (SEP), imbalanced diet and microbial dysbiosis 3,4 . Lower SEP is a key factor which has previously been associated with higher risks of mortality and incident CVD and renal disease, where lifestyle factors, such as smoking history and diet, may also parIally mediate associaIons of SEP with mortality and HF.

The clinical implicaIons of the findings from Wei et al, emphasise the growing importance of the link between the diet, the microbiota and HF risk. Measurement of PAGln levels may enable enhanced clinical prognosis in predicIng the risk of HF, independently of tradiIonal risk factors, renal funcIon, and NT-proBNP levels. AddiIonally, it may open a route to using 'Food as Medicine' to modify disease predisposiIon and progression, through manipulaIon of the composiIon of the microbiome 10 . This has already shown promise in the treatment of CKD and is a simple addiIon to the physicians armamentarium should it show similar promise for HF.
